subtitle: A western with giant machines

body: Wild Guns is Natsume’s Super Nintendo shooting-gallery game, combining a revenge story from the Wild West with robots and science-fiction machinery. Annie enlists the bounty hunter Clint after her family is killed, and either character can be controlled through the adventure. They move across the foreground while firing at enemies farther into the scene. A second player can join cooperatively. The resulting action combines the spectacle of an arcade shooting gallery with a vulnerable character whose position remains under the player’s control.

The character and the target do not occupy the same depth. Enemies appear across the background while Annie or Clint must evade attacks in front, sidestepping and jumping as the fight develops. Watching only the reticle leaves the character exposed; watching only the character wastes opportunities to clear the scene. That division gives even a fixed viewpoint a demanding sense of movement. The player has to coordinate where shots are going with where the next incoming attack will arrive, often in the company of a cooperative partner.

Six levels organise their action into encounters that build toward larger enemies and bosses. Natsume’s small development team gives the western setting a distinctive mechanical scale, placing familiar frontier imagery beside exaggerated machines. The cooperative mode shares that screen with another player, while target practice provides a separate score competition. These modes use the same clear relationship between the foreground fighters and their distant targets. Wild Guns finds variety in what enters the scene and how its fire forces the characters to move.
